analogy.p: Imagine two people who speak different languages: a conversion factor is a translator who tells you how many words in one language equal one word in the other. You cannot add a number of 'metres' to a number of 'centimetres' any more than you can add French and German words without translating first. Squaring the factor for area is like translating a whole sentence of two words: each of the two lengths has to be translated, so the factor is applied twice. The analogy breaks down because translators are not exact, whereas metric conversion factors are exact powers of ten (although imperial equivalents are approximate).

bullets: A **unit** says what you are measuring in (cm, kg, hours). A **conversion factor** is the number that links two units, for example 1 km = 1000 m.
You need the standard metric relationships from memory: they are not given on the Edexcel formula sheet.

You also need the **rough metric equivalents of everyday imperial units** (miles, feet, pounds, pints, gallons); questions normally give the exact factor, but you should know whether the answer is sensible.
**Numerical context** means converting actual values (e.g. 3.2 km to m). **Algebraic context** means converting expressions (e.g. x cm to metres is x ÷ 100).
Conversions appear inside other questions: area and volume of shapes, speed, density, pressure, best buys, exchange rates and scale drawings.
Calculator and non-calculator papers both test this, so the factors must be secure and the arithmetic quick (multiplying and dividing by 10, 100, 1000).
core.h: What the specification asks you to do
core.p: The Edexcel specification (Ratio, proportion and rates of change) says you must be able to **change freely between related standard units** (time, length, area, volume/capacity and mass) and **between compound units** (speed, rates of pay, prices, density, pressure) in **numerical and algebraic contexts**. This is a skill that sits underneath nearly every other topic: if your units do not match, the answer is wrong even when your method is perfect. Examiners reward the first mark for a correct conversion factor and the last mark for a sensible unit on the answer.

bullets: **kilo** (k) means ×1000, so 1 km = 1000 m and 1 kg = 1000 g.
**centi** (c) means ÷100, so 1 cm = 0.01 m (100 cm = 1 m).
**milli** (m) means ÷1000, so 1 mm = 0.001 m (1000 mm = 1 m) and 1 ml = 0.001 litre.
1 litre = 1000 ml = 100 cl, and 1 litre = 1000 cm³ (so 1 ml = 1 cm³).
Standard form links to this: 1 km = 1 × 10³ m, 1 mm = 1 × 10⁻³ m.
Higher tier extension: you may be asked to give answers in standard form after converting (e.g. 0.00042 km = 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ km = 0.42 m = 4.2 × 10² mm).
core.p: The metric system is built on **base units** (metre for length, gram or kilogram for mass, litre for capacity, second for time) combined with **prefixes** that scale them by powers of ten. Because it is decimal, converting means moving the decimal point, which is why it is so much easier than imperial. Learning what each prefix stands for lets you rebuild any conversion rather than memorise a long list.

bullets: Worked pattern: 3.7 km to m. Km is bigger than m, so the number gets bigger: 3.7 × 1000 = 3700 m.
Worked pattern: 450 mm to m. Mm is smaller than m, so the number gets smaller: 450 ÷ 1000 = 0.45 m.
Worked pattern: 2.5 kg to g: 2.5 × 1000 = 2500 g. And 750 g to kg: 750 ÷ 1000 = 0.75 kg.
Worked pattern: 0.6 litres to ml: 0.6 × 1000 = 600 ml.
For a two-step conversion (km to cm) multiply by each factor in turn: 1 km = 1000 m = 1000 × 100 = 100 000 cm.
Lining up place values helps: 0.045 kg → 45 g because the decimal point moves three places to the right.
When adding or comparing quantities, **convert everything to the same unit first**, then calculate.
Link to other topics: a perimeter question with sides given in cm and m must be converted before you add them.
core.p: For one-dimensional measures the rule is simple: if you go from a **bigger unit to a smaller unit** the number gets **bigger**, so you **multiply**; from a **smaller unit to a bigger unit** the number gets **smaller**, so you **divide**. Always ask yourself whether the answer should be larger or smaller than the starting number before you decide which operation to use. This single check catches most conversion errors.

bullets: 1 hour = 60 minutes = 3600 seconds, and 1 day = 24 hours = 1440 minutes = 86 400 seconds.
**Minutes to hours: divide by 60.** 15 min = 15 ÷ 60 = 0.25 h; 20 min = 1/3 h = 0.333… h (leave it as a fraction or use 20/60 to stay exact).
**Hours to minutes: multiply by 60.** 0.35 h × 60 = 21 min; 2.4 h = 2 h + 0.4 × 60 min = 2 h 24 min.
1 h 24 min = 1 + 24/60 = 1.4 hours. It is **not** 1.24 hours.
Quarter of an hour = 15 min = 0.25 h; half an hour = 0.5 h; three-quarters = 45 min = 0.75 h.
Time differences: from 09:45 to 13:20 count up in chunks (09:45 → 10:00 is 15 min, 10:00 → 13:00 is 3 h, 13:00 → 13:20 is 20 min) to get 3 h 35 min.
12-hour and 24-hour clock: 15:40 is 3:40 pm; add 12 to pm times to get the 24-hour time.
Calculators: use the degrees-minutes-seconds button (° ' ") on many models to convert decimal hours to hours and minutes quickly, but know how to do it by hand.
core.h: Time is not a decimal system
core.p: Time is the one common measure that is **not** based on powers of ten. There are **60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour, 24 hours in a day** and 7 days in a week. A very common loss of marks comes from treating minutes as if they were hundredths of an hour. To use time in a calculation (especially speed) you usually need **decimal hours**, so you must convert carefully.

bullets: 1 hectare (ha) = 10 000 m² (a 100 m by 100 m square). This is used for land.
To go from m² to cm² multiply by 10 000; from cm² to m² divide by 10 000. Example: 3.5 m² = 35 000 cm²; 8500 cm² = 0.85 m².
Alternative method: convert the **lengths first**, then work out the area. A rectangle 2 m by 50 cm: convert to 200 cm by 50 cm, area = 10 000 cm².
Common error: multiplying by 100 only. Always test with the 1 m by 1 m square picture.
The same squared rule applies to any pair of length units; if a factor between two area units is not given, square the length factor yourself.
core.p: Area is measured in **square units**, so the conversion factor for length must be **squared**. This is the biggest trap in the topic: although 1 m = 100 cm, one square metre is **not** 100 cm². Picture a square with sides 1 m: each side is 100 cm, so the area is 100 × 100 = **10 000 cm²**. The same reasoning works for any pair of units.

bullets: **1 ml = 1 cm³**, and **1 litre = 1000 ml = 1000 cm³**.
**1 m³ = 1000 litres** (1 000 000 cm³ ÷ 1000 cm³ per litre).
Example: a tank 50 cm by 40 cm by 30 cm has volume 60 000 cm³ = 60 000 ml = 60 litres.
Example: a pool holding 12 m³ of water holds 12 × 1000 = 12 000 litres.
To go from cm³ to m³, divide by 1 000 000; from m³ to cm³, multiply by 1 000 000.
Link to other topics: volume of prisms and cylinders, density (mass = density × volume) and water-flow problems all need these conversions.
core.p: Volume is measured in **cubic units**, so the length factor is **cubed**. A cube of side 1 m is 100 cm × 100 cm × 100 cm = **1 000 000 cm³**. **Capacity** is the amount a container holds and is measured in litres and millilitres; it connects to volume through the key fact **1 ml = 1 cm³**. This is how a 3D shape question turns into a litres answer.

bullets: km/h to m/s: multiply by 1000 (km to m) and divide by 3600 (hours to seconds), which is the same as **dividing by 3.6**. 72 km/h = 72 ÷ 3.6 = 20 m/s.
m/s to km/h: **multiply by 3.6**. 15 m/s = 54 km/h.
Write out the steps in full if you are unsure: 72 km/h = 72 000 m per hour = 72 000 ÷ 3600 = 20 m per second.
Speed in miles per hour (mph) to km/h: use 1 mile ≈ 1.6 km. 30 mph ≈ 48 km/h.
Quick sense check: m/s numbers are **smaller** than km/h numbers (a car at 70 km/h is about 19 m/s).
Other compound examples: litres per minute to cm³ per second (× 1000 ÷ 60) and prices per 100 g to prices per kg (× 10).
Method for any compound conversion: write the rate as a fraction with units, multiply by conversion fractions equal to 1, and cancel units.
Higher tier extension: you may need to convert and then use the result in a formula, e.g. distance = speed × time with the time given in minutes.
core.p: A compound unit has **two units joined by 'per'**, so you must convert the top unit and the bottom unit **separately**. For speed, convert the distance (km → m) and the time (hours → seconds) in turn. The standard result is that 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h, because there are 3600 seconds in an hour and 1000 m in a km. This is the most commonly examined compound conversion.

bullets: **1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.** So 7.8 g/cm³ = 7800 kg/m³ and 0.9 g/cm³ = 900 kg/m³.
Reverse: kg/m³ ÷ 1000 = g/cm³ (e.g. 2700 kg/m³ = 2.7 g/cm³).
Pressure is force per area: **1 N/cm² = 10 000 N/m²** because 1 m² = 10 000 cm².
The pascal: 1 Pa = 1 N/m². So 2 N/cm² = 20 000 Pa.
Always check the units given before using a formula: if density is in g/cm³, volume must be in cm³ and mass in g.
Tip: convert the **measurements** to match the density unit before multiplying, rather than converting at the end.
Link to other topics: Physics (density and pressure) and Chemistry use the same conversions.
core.p: Density (mass ÷ volume) and pressure (force ÷ area) are compound units whose **bottom unit is a square or cube**, so the length factor is squared or cubed in the denominator. Converting from g/cm³ to kg/m³ changes the top unit by ÷1000 (g to kg) and the bottom unit by ÷1 000 000 (cm³ to m³), giving an overall ×1000. Working through the steps is safer than learning the factor blindly.

bullets: Sense check: if one pound buys more than one euro, then the number of euros must be bigger than the number of pounds.
Comparing prices abroad: convert both to the **same currency** before deciding which is cheaper.
Round money to **2 decimal places** (pence/cents) at the end of the calculation, not in the middle.
Rates can be given as 'X per £1' or '£1 = X' or as a table; read it carefully and write down which way it works.
If a fee or commission is given as a percentage, read the question carefully to see whether it applies before or after the conversion.
Link to other topics: percentages (fees), ratio, and best-buy problems.
core.p: Currency conversion is a unit conversion where the factor is the **exchange rate**. Rates are written as '£1 = €1.20', meaning one pound is worth 1.20 euros. The method is always the same: **multiply** to convert into the currency with the **bigger number** (a pound buys more euros than 1) and **divide** to convert back. Writing the rate as a ratio and checking the direction prevents the commonest slip.

bullets: Length: 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm (exactly 2.54 cm); 1 foot ≈ 30 cm; 1 mile ≈ 1.6 km; 5 miles ≈ 8 km.
Mass: 1 kg ≈ 2.2 pounds (lb); 1 pound ≈ 450 g; 1 ounce ≈ 28 g.
Capacity: 1 litre ≈ 1.75 pints; 1 gallon ≈ 4.5 litres.
Within imperial: 12 inches = 1 foot, 3 feet = 1 yard, 1760 yards = 1 mile, 16 ounces = 1 pound, 14 pounds = 1 stone, 8 pints = 1 gallon.
Method: multiply or divide by the given factor and use common sense on which way it goes: 10 miles is about 16 km (more km than miles).
Example: 5 gallons ≈ 5 × 4.5 = 22.5 litres.
Imperial conversions give approximate answers, so use the approximately-equal sign and give a reasonable degree of accuracy.
Real-world use: road signs in mph, recipes in ounces, heights in feet and inches, and fuel consumption in miles per gallon.
core.p: The specification also expects you to know **rough metric equivalents** of everyday imperial measures. Exam questions normally give the exact factor if you need it, but knowing the approximate values means you can check whether an answer is reasonable. The relationships between imperial units themselves (for example 12 inches in a foot) are not always provided, so know the common ones.

bullets: x cm in metres = x ÷ 100 = x/100 m. 3x metres in cm = 300x cm.
A rectangle with sides x m and 50 cm: convert 50 cm to 0.5 m, area = 0.5x m², or convert x m to 100x cm and the area is 5000x cm².
A speed of v km/h in m/s is v ÷ 3.6 = 5v/18 m/s.
A tank of volume V m³ holds 1000V litres.
A price of p pence per gram is 1000p pence per kg, which is £10p per kg (dividing by 100 to change pence to pounds).
Always show a conversion line so that you earn the method mark even if the algebra slips.
Check dimensional consistency: if you multiply two lengths you must get an area; this helps spot a wrong power.
Higher tier extension: set up an equation after converting, e.g. area = 0.75 m² means 7500 cm², so x × 50 = 7500 gives x = 150 cm.
core.p: In algebraic questions the numbers are replaced by letters or expressions, but the method is identical: decide whether the number should get bigger or smaller and multiply or divide by the factor. The answer is an **expression**, not a number. You must also keep the area and volume factors squared or cubed. These questions test whether you really understand why the factors work.

bullets: Always write the unit on the final answer; a missing unit often loses the accuracy mark.
Use estimation to check: a person's height of 1.7 m is 170 cm, not 17 cm or 1700 cm.
Typical sizes help: a mug holds about 300 ml, a car about 1500 kg, a door about 2 m high, a walking pace is about 5 km/h.
If an exact value is converted, give an exact answer (e.g. 0.45 m); if the factor is approximate, round (e.g. ≈ 22.5 litres).
Do not round part-way through; keep full calculator values and round at the end.
If asked for the answer 'in standard form' convert first, then express as A × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ A < 10.
If a question gives mixed units, rewrite every value in a single unit at the start and keep a clear working column.
Link to other topics: error intervals and bounds use units too (e.g. 4.5 ≤ length < 5.5 m).
core.h: Choosing sensible units, accuracy and rounding
core.p: Part of the skill is selecting an appropriate unit and presenting the answer sensibly. The answer should have the **unit requested** and a degree of accuracy that suits the context. A conversion by a factor of 10, 100 or 1000 is exact, but conversions using rounded factors (such as 1 mile ≈ 1.6 km) are only approximate and the answer should be rounded sensibly.

bullets: **Geometry**: perimeter, area, surface area and volume of shapes with mixed units; scale drawings and maps (scale factors are ratios, e.g. 1 : 50 000 means 1 cm represents 50 000 cm = 500 m = 0.5 km).
**Ratio and proportion**: best buys require converting to the same unit price (e.g. pence per 100 g).
**Rates of change**: speed, density, pressure, flow rate (litres per minute).
**Number**: standard form to express very large and small measurements.
**Real-life**: hours and minutes in time-sheets, rates of pay, exchange rates and recipes.
**Science**: Physics and Chemistry use exactly the same unit conversions, for example cm³ to dm³ and g to kg.
Exam strategy: underline the units asked for in the question, write them at the end of every line of working, and check the final unit matches.
core.h: Link to other topics and Higher tier application
core.p: Because conversions are fundamental, they are used throughout the course. Higher tier questions typically hide the conversion inside a longer multi-step problem and award marks for it at the start. Recognising when a conversion is needed is half the battle.

exam: Command words: **'Convert'** or **'Change'** means state the new value with its unit; **'Work out'** may hide a conversion inside a longer question, so scan for mixed units.

Typical mark allocation: 1 mark for a correct simple conversion (e.g. 2.5 km in m); 2 marks for an area/volume or two-step conversion; 3 to 4 marks when the conversion is part of a multi-step problem such as speed, density or best buy.
Method mark: show the conversion factor you are using (e.g. × 10 000) even if you slip in the arithmetic.
Write the unit on every line of working. This helps you spot unit errors and often earns the accuracy mark.
For area and volume, either convert the lengths first or use the squared/cubed factor. Say which in your working.
For speed questions, make the units match: if the time is in minutes and the speed is in km/h, change minutes to hours (÷ 60) first.
For exchange rate questions state 'multiply' or 'divide' and give the answer to 2 decimal places for money.
Use the sense check: re-read the question and ask whether your answer is the right size (a person is not 17 m tall).
For algebraic conversions give a simplified expression (e.g. 5v/18 m/s) and not a decimal rounded early.
If a conversion factor is given in the question, use that exact value rather than a different one from memory.
Write 'approximately' (≈) for answers using rounded imperial factors, and round at the end only.

mistakes.r: Area factors are squared: 1 m² = 100 × 100 = 10 000 cm². Volume factors are cubed: 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³.
mistakes.w: Multiplying by 100 to change m² into cm².

mistakes.r: Minutes are out of 60, so 30 min = 0.5 h and 1 h 30 min = 1.5 hours.
Decide first: going to a smaller unit gives a bigger number (multiply); going to a bigger unit gives a smaller number (divide).
mistakes.w: Multiplying when you should divide (or the reverse) in a conversion.

mistakes.r: Both parts change: multiply by 1000 for km → m and divide by 3600 for h → s, so overall divide by 3.6.
mistakes.w: Dividing by 3600 only when changing km/h to m/s.

mistakes.r: 1 litre = 1000 ml = 1000 cm³, so 1 ml = 1 cm³.
mistakes.w: Using 1 litre = 100 cm³ or 1 ml = 10 cm³.

mistakes.r: Multiply to go from £ to €, divide to go from € to £, and check that € should be the bigger number.
mistakes.w: Converting exchange rate the wrong way, so £ come out larger than euros when the rate is £1 = €1.20.

mistakes.r: Convert everything to one unit at the start, then do the calculation.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to convert all values to the same unit before calculating.

mistakes.r: Write the unit asked for; examiners withhold the final mark if the unit is missing or wrong.
mistakes.w: Leaving off the unit or giving the wrong unit on the final answer.

mistakes.r: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³ (g to kg ÷1000, cm³ to m³ ÷1 000 000).

summary: Edexcel requires you to change freely between related standard units of time, length, area, volume or capacity and mass, and between compound units such as speed, density and pressure, in numerical and algebraic contexts. It matters because nearly every measurement question loses marks if the units do not match, and the squared and cubed factors for area and volume are a favourite trap.

terms.d: A standard quantity used to measure something, e.g. metre, gram, second, litre.
The number you multiply or divide by to change from one unit to another, e.g. 1 km = 1000 m.
A decimal system of units based on powers of 10, with prefixes such as kilo, centi and milli.
A word-part that scales a base unit, e.g. kilo = ×1000, centi = ÷100, milli = ÷1000.
The amount of liquid a container can hold, measured in litres or millilitres; 1 ml = 1 cm³.
A unit made from two or more units combined by 'per' or multiplication, e.g. km/h, g/cm³, N/m².
The distance travelled per unit of time, e.g. km/h or m/s.
The mass of a substance per unit volume, e.g. g/cm³ or kg/m³.
The force acting per unit area, e.g. N/m² (pascal, Pa).
The amount of one currency that equals one unit of another, e.g. £1 = €1.20.
Older units used in the UK such as miles, pounds, pints and gallons, with non-decimal relationships.
A unit of land area equal to 10 000 m².
A number written as A × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer.
A quick estimate to see whether an answer is the right size and in the right direction.

worked.q: A rectangular patio measures 2.4 m by 1.5 m. Work out its area in cm². (3 marks)
steps: Convert lengths to cm: 2.4 m = 240 cm and 1.5 m = 150 cm (× 100). [M1]
Check using the area factor: area in m² = 2.4 × 1.5 = 3.6 m²; 3.6 × 10 000 = 36 000 cm² ✓.
